title: Fifth commandment: health (CCC 2288–2301)
hookLine: care for health, and respect for the dead

cards: Goal reached, ten thousand steps, says the wristband. Down the street, another man hasn't seen a doctor in six years and jokes that his body will let him know.
And in an old story from the Bible, a man named Tobit leaves his dinner untasted, goes out, and carries home the body of a murdered man lying in the street, so he can bury him after sunset.
Three ways of treating a body, living and dead.

teach.b: The Catechism calls life and physical health precious gifts entrusted to us by God. So we take reasonable care of them, keeping in mind the needs of others and the common good.
Society, it adds, should help people find food, clothing, housing, health care, schooling and work. Health is never only private. Then a sharp turn.
Morality respects bodily life but doesn't make it an absolute.

teach.h: NOT A CULT OF THE BODY.
teach.b: The Catechism rejects what it calls a cult of the body: sacrificing everything for it, idolizing physical perfection and success at sports. The body is a gift to care for, not a god to serve.
In between sits temperance: avoiding every kind of excess, the abuse of food, alcohol, tobacco or medicine.

Those who put others in danger by drunkenness or reckless speed, it says plainly, are gravely guilty, and using drugs, except on strictly medical grounds, is a grave offense. Then it follows the body to the end.
The dying should be given attention and care, to live their last moments in dignity and peace, surrounded by prayer.
The bodies of the dead must be treated with respect and charity, in faith and hope of the resurrection; burying the dead is a work of mercy.
That's Tobit, whose journey you followed in year two, leaving his dinner to carry a dead man home.
Organ donation after death can be a noble act, and cremation is permitted, as long as it isn't chosen as a denial of faith in the resurrection.
From the gym to the graveside: care for the body, honor it, but don't worship it.

how: Catholics are taught to care for their health with temperance, to accompany the dying with prayer and the sacraments, and to bury the dead with a funeral Mass, a corporal work of mercy.

o: a rule only about not harming others
caring for the body without worshiping it
keeping the body perfect at any cost

games.q: the body, living and dead — tap the pairs.
p: a precious gift entrusted by God

s: the Catechism treats bodily life as the highest value
it says morality respects bodily life but doesn't make it an absolute.
as long as it isn't chosen as a denial of faith in the resurrection.
the Catechism calls burying the dead a work of mercy
the bodies of the dead are treated with respect, in hope of the resurrection.

games.q: you're Tobit, sitting down to a good dinner. word comes that a murdered man's body is lying in the street. what do you do?
o: finish your dinner; it isn't your business.
get up, bring the body in, and bury it after dark.
report it and go to bed.
games.why: in the book of Tobit, he leaves his food, takes the body in, and buries it when the sun has set.

practice: Starting at your feet, move your attention slowly upward and notice each part without judging it: tension, tiredness, hunger, pain.
Choose one small, reasonable kindness for your body today: a glass of water, a walk, an early night, the appointment you keep putting off.
If you pray, thank God for this body as a gift; if not, thank it plainly for carrying you this far.

wordCard.voice: Fifth commandment. Respect for life includes reasonable care for health, temperance, and respect for the dying and the dead, without making the body an idol. Today's word.

carryVoice: Your line: care, not worship. Living or dead, the body is owed respect. I'll be here tomorrow.
